details:
**Transubstantiation**
The Catholic doctrine that during the Eucharist the substance of the bread and wine truly becomes the body and blood of Christ, while their "accidents" (appearance, taste) remain, using Aristotelian categories. The Eastern Orthodox use the related Greek term "metousiosis."

**Last Supper**
The final meal Jesus shared with his apostles on the night he was betrayed, which the Eucharist commemorates and re-enacts. At it, he blessed bread and wine, called them his body and blood, and commanded "Do this in remembrance of me." It is commemorated on Holy (Maundy) Thursday.

**Real Presence**
The belief that Christ is truly, not just symbolically, present in the Eucharistic bread and wine. Catholics explain it through transubstantiation; Lutherans hold a "sacramental union" in which Christ is present "in, with, and under" the bread and wine (sometimes called consubstantiation); many other Protestants see the rite as a symbolic memorial.

**Marburg Colloquy**
A 1529 meeting where Martin Luther and Ulrich (Huldrych) Zwingli tried to unite the Protestant movement. They agreed on most points but split over the Eucharist: Luther insisted on the Real Presence, while Zwingli saw the rite as symbolic.

**Fourth Lateran Council**
The 1215 church council under Pope Innocent III that formally used and defined the term "transubstantiation." The Council of Trent reaffirmed the doctrine in the 16th century against Protestant objections.

**Anaphora (Eucharistic Prayer)**
The central consecration prayer of the Eucharist, especially in Eastern churches. It includes the anamnesis (a remembrance of Christ's saving acts) and the epiclesis (calling the Holy Spirit down on the gifts); common Orthodox versions are attributed to St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil.

**Words of Institution**
The words of Jesus repeated by the priest over the bread and wine, such as "This is my body" (Latin "Hoc est enim corpus meum") and "This is my blood" and "Do this in memory of me." They are drawn from 1 Corinthians 11:23–25 and the Gospels (e.g., Matthew 26 and Mark 14).

**Holy Qurbana**
The name for the Eucharist in Syriac Christian traditions, meaning "offering" or "sacrifice." It is associated with the ancient Liturgy of St. James.

**Bread (host, prosphora)**
The element representing Christ's body. Catholics use unleavened wafers (hosts); the Orthodox use leavened prosphora stamped with a seal (sphragis) bearing letters for "Jesus Christ conquers." Catholics sing the Agnus Dei during the Fraction Rite, when the host is broken.

**Melchizedek**
The priest-king of Salem who brings out bread and wine and blesses Abraham in Genesis 14. Church Fathers such as Clement of Alexandria, and later Thomas Aquinas, saw this offering as a prefiguration of the Eucharist.

**Agape feasts (love feasts)**
Communal meals held by early Christians, at which the Eucharist was originally celebrated. The two were later separated, and figures such as St. Augustine criticized holding the rite at such feasts.

**Foot washing**
A practice that precedes communion among groups such as Mennonites and Seventh-day Adventists, imitating Jesus washing the disciples' feet at the Last Supper. Adventists hold communion quarterly as an "open" rite available to non-members.

**Quam Singulari and First Communion**
A 1910 decree of Pope Pius X that allowed children to receive communion once they reach the "age of reason," around seven. Catholic children usually make their first confession (Reconciliation) first, and girls often wear white dresses resembling wedding gowns for First Communion.

**Monstrance and Eucharistic adoration**
A monstrance is an ornate vessel, often sunburst-shaped, used to display the consecrated host. Catholics use it for adoration of the Blessed Sacrament, which hymns like "Ave verum corpus" honor.

**Mustum, intinction, and the Didache**
Mustum is barely fermented grape juice permitted in place of wine; many Protestants use plain grape juice. Intinction is dipping the bread into the wine before receiving it. The Didache, an early Christian text, gives Eucharistic prayers in which the cup comes before the bread.
